# Larkholm Island Council: ferry renewal briefing note

This is a fictional briefing note written for a scenario-simulation demonstration. All names, places and figures are invented.

## Background

The island's only ferry, the diesel vessel MV Gannet, is 27 years old. Its maintenance bill has risen every year since 2021, and the operating contract with the Larkholm Ferry Company ends in 2028.

## Usage

Council counts show 412,000 one-way crossings in 2025. Of these, 61% took place between June and September.

## Options before the Council

Option 1 is a diesel refit costing $3.1 million, which would extend the vessel's life by about eight years. Option 2 is a battery-electric replacement costing $14.2 million. The national Clean Coasts Fund would pay 40% of the electric vessel's cost if the Council commits before 30 September.

## Council constraints

The Finance Committee will not raise the annual ferry subsidy above $1.8 million. Any decision to buy a new vessel needs evidence of sustained use and a funding plan before the March budget vote. Councillors from the harbour ward have said they will not back a plan that cuts winter service for islanders.

## Timeline and open questions

The grant deadline is 30 September. Grid upgrades for charging at both terminals are expected to take 14 to 18 months, and the diesel vessel would keep running throughout. Officers have not yet agreed how the cost of the charging upgrades would be shared. The operator has proposed a fare increase to cover part of that cost; the Council has not taken a position on the size of any increase.

# Larkholm Ferry Company: electric ferry feasibility memo

This is a fictional memo written for a scenario-simulation demonstration. All names, places and figures are invented.

## Ridership

Our ticketing system recorded 365,000 one-way crossings in 2025. About 58% of them were between June and September.

## What an electric ferry would change

A battery-electric vessel would cut fuel use and operating emissions on the route by about 90% and save roughly $0.9 million a year in fuel. Charging at both terminals needs grid upgrades that will take 14 to 18 months, so the diesel vessel must keep sailing until they are finished.

## Our proposal

To protect the battery and leave time for charging, we propose a reduced winter timetable of four daily return sailings from November to March, instead of today's six. We also propose a 12% fare increase to help pay for the charging equipment.

## Risks we want the Council to understand

Battery vessels have less power in reserve in heavy weather, so more winter sailings may be cancelled in storms. If the grant deadline is missed, the electric option is unlikely to be affordable. We do not yet know how many islanders will accept fewer winter sailings, and we have not surveyed them.

documents.name: 03-residents-survey-summary.md
documents.content:
# Larkholm Residents' Association: ferry survey summary

This is a fictional survey summary written for a scenario-simulation demonstration. All names, places and figures are invented.

## Who answered

The Association surveyed 1,150 islander households and received replies from 52% of them.

## What islanders said

68% of respondents ranked year-round reliability above emissions reductions. 71% oppose a reduced winter timetable, and 64% oppose a 12% fare increase. 52% said they would support an electric ferry if six sailings a day were kept in winter.

## Who depends on the ferry in winter

The Larkholm Health Centre reports about 140 patient trips a month to mainland clinics between November and March, including dialysis appointments that cannot be rescheduled. Many nurses, teachers and shift workers commute by the first and last sailings of the day.

## What the Association asks

The Association asks the Council to guarantee at least six winter sailings a day and to cap any fare increase at 5%. It will not oppose an electric ferry that meets these two conditions.

documents.content:
# Stakeholder statements on the ferry proposal

This is a fictional collection of statements written for a scenario-simulation demonstration. All names, places and figures are invented.

## Green Tide Alliance

The Alliance polled 400 visitors and residents and found that 74% support an electric ferry. The Alliance states that islanders overwhelmingly prefer the electric ferry even with fewer winter sailings. It estimates that the diesel ferry emits about 2,900 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year and urges the Council to accept the Clean Coasts Fund grant before 30 September. It proposes paying for winter service from summer fares.

## Harbour Business Council

Visitors account for about 70% of summer crossings, and summer visitor spending is worth around $9.5 million a year to island shops, guest houses and cafes. The Business Council supports an electric ferry because it would strengthen the island's green image. It warns that any fare increase above 5% would reduce day-trip bookings and asks that construction never disrupt the June to September season. It wants eight summer sailings a day.

documents.content:
# Scenario assumptions (analyst-provided)

This is a fictional set of planning assumptions written for a scenario-simulation demonstration. They are inputs chosen by the analyst, not facts from any source.

- A1. The Council commits to the electric ferry before the grant deadline, so the Clean Coasts Fund pays 40% of the vessel cost.
- A2. Fares rise by 12% when the electric ferry enters service.
- A3. From November to March the timetable is cut from six to four daily return sailings.
- A4. Charging works finish about 16 months after the decision, and the diesel vessel keeps sailing until then.
- A5. No new subsidy is available beyond the current $1.8 million ceiling.
- A6. Stakeholders learn about decisions through a broadcast notice board that everyone sees and through smaller topic communities where like-minded people talk.

These assumptions frame the what-if question. They are not predictions, and the simulation does not test whether they are realistic.

report.title: Stakeholder Responses to Larkholm's Ferry Transition and Winter Timetable Changes
report.executiveSummary: Simulation of stakeholder responses on Larkholm Island to replacing the diesel ferry with a battery-electric vessel coupled with a reduced winter timetable (from six to four daily return sailings) shows initial divided reactions evolving into overall strong support by round six, with an average final support share of approximately 83% and zero recorded opposition. The proposed 12% fare increase to fund charging infrastructure faces substantial resistance, with calls to cap fare rises at 5% to maintain affordability. Key stakeholders—including council members, ferry operators, residents' associations, and environmental groups—advocate for maintaining at least six winter sailings and limiting fare increases, seeking funding solutions such as reallocating summer revenues or securing grants. Simulation interactions reveal that despite an initial dip in support following announcement of the reduced winter timetable, opinion recovers and stabilizes with decreasing polarization, reflecting ongoing dialogue and compromise efforts. sections.title: Community Perspectives on Battery-Electric Ferry Adoption
sections.body:
Fictional stakeholders on Larkholm Island show a complex but ultimately supportive response to replacing the diesel ferry with a battery-electric vessel paired with a reduced winter timetable. Initial reactions feature a mix of support and opposition centered on concerns about winter service reductions and fare increases. By the sixth round of simulated discussion, overall support rises to about 83%, with no recorded opposition, suggesting wide acceptance of the electric ferry if key community priorities are met.

The diesel ferry MV Gannet currently handles 412,000 one-way crossings per year, 61% during summer months (S1). Due to rising maintenance costs, the council is evaluating a $3.1 million diesel refit or a $14.2 million battery-electric ferry replacement, the latter eligible for a 40% Clean Coasts Fund grant if approved before the deadline (S1). The ferry company estimates the electric ferry would cut fuel use and emissions by about 90%, saving roughly $0.9 million annually (S3). To preserve battery health and accommodate necessary grid upgrades taking 14-18 months, the operator proposes reducing winter sailings from six to four daily return trips between November and March (S3).

Island residents prioritize reliable year-round ferry service over emissions reductions, with 68% ranking reliability top and 71% opposing reduced winter sailings (S5). A majority (64%) also opposes the 12% fare increase proposed to fund charging infrastructure, preferring fare rises capped at 5%. More than half (52%) support the electric ferry if six winter sailings are maintained (S5). Regular winter users include patients needing ongoing mainland healthcare such as dialysis, as well as nurses and shift workers commuting on the first and last sailings (S5).

Council members from the harbour ward strongly support the electric ferry for environmental and cost advantages but insist on maintaining six daily winter sailings and limiting fare increases to 5% to ensure political viability and rider affordability (I1, M-community-1-agent-1, M-community-5-agent-1). They intend to secure grant funding and explore alternative financial options to uphold winter services within the $1.8 million subsidy limit (S1, I1).

The ferry operator endorses the electric ferry and explains the winter sailing reduction as necessary during the grid upgrade period, committing to minimize fare impact and engage with community concerns for a smooth transition (M-plaza-1-agent-2, M-community-6-agent-2). Environmental group Green Tide Alliance supports emissions reductions but proposes funding some winter operations from summer revenues, suggesting at least five daily winter sailings and fare increases capped at 10% (M-community-4-agent-4).

Local business voices support the electric ferry for sustainability but warn that the 12% fare hike and reduced winter service could damage visitor numbers and economic health, advocating a fare rise below 5% and maintaining winter service to sustain year-round trade (M-plaza-5-agent-5, M-community-3-agent-5).

Simulated discussions reveal early high polarization with about equal support and opposition, especially following the announcement of winter service reductions. Support scores drop to around 50% in rounds 4 and 5 but recover to an 83% support share and zero opposition by round 6 as dialogue leads to compromise (S7). The polarization measure declines over time, reflecting a community reaching consensus.

In conclusion, Larkholm stakeholders generally accept the battery-electric ferry replacement provided six winter sailings are preserved and fare increases kept near 5%. This reflects a balanced community emphasis on sustainability benefits alongside critical year-round accessibility and affordability. Successful transition depends on transparent negotiation, innovative funding, and sensitivity to stakeholders’ essential service needs.

sections.title: Economic Impacts on Harbour Businesses and Local Commerce
sections.body:
The fictional stakeholders on Larkholm Island exhibit a complex but evolving response to the proposal to replace the island ferry's diesel vessel with a battery-electric ferry alongside a reduction in winter sailings. Initial reactions show significant division: support for the environmental and cost-saving benefits of the electric ferry coexists with strong community concerns regarding the proposed cutback of winter sailings from six to four daily return trips and a 12% fare increase.

Island residents prioritize year-round reliability above emissions reductions, with a survey reporting that 68% ranked year-round reliability highest and 71% opposing the reduction of winter sailings (S5). The winter ferry service is critical for access to healthcare—such as approximately 140 patient trips monthly to mainland clinics during winter, including non-reschedulable dialysis treatments—and for workers commuting shifts, which explains strong resistance to reduced winter frequency (S5).

The proposed $14.2 million battery-electric vessel, supported by a 40% national grant conditional on timely commitment, offers approximately $0.9 million annual fuel savings and a 90% cut in fuel-related emissions (S3). However, the charging infrastructure upgrade will take 14 to 18 months, during which diesel service continues; to protect battery life and accommodate charging schedules, a reduced winter timetable is recommended by the ferry operator (S3).

Key stakeholder voices illustrate the balance of interests:

- The ferry operator (M-plaza-1-agent-2, M-community-6-agent-2) consistently supports the electric ferry for its sustainability and operational savings but acknowledges the necessity of managing community concerns about winter service cuts and fare increases. They advocate four winter sailings as a compromise reflecting technical realities.

- The Council, represented by agent-1, supports the electric ferry contingent on maintaining at least six daily winter sailings and limiting fare increases to under 5% to keep the service affordable and politically sustainable. The Council is active in pursuing alternative funding strategies, including possible reallocation of summer revenues, and is concerned that cutting winter service risks alienating constituents (I1, M-community-1-agent-1, M-community-5-agent-1).

- Residents’ Association leadership (agent-3) strongly endorses an electric ferry but demands a minimal six sailings daily winter schedule and a fare increase capped at 5% to protect residents’ needs, particularly emphasizing access to healthcare and essential work. They reject the proposed 12% fare rise and reduced winter timetable as untenable (I2, M-community-1-agent-3).

- Environmental advocates, such as the Green Tide Alliance (agent-4), emphasize emissions reductions but propose funding compromises like using summer fare revenues to partially support winter service, suggesting a minimum of five sailings with a fare increase no greater than 10% (M-community-4-agent-4).

Community discussion and simulated interactions reveal an initial decline in average support following announcement of the reduced winter schedule in round 4, with mean opinion dropping notably and polarization temporarily increasing. However, by the final rounds, support rebounds and stabilizes with minimal opposition and substantially reduced polarization, indicating convergence through dialogue (timeline/plaza rounds 4 to 6; timeline/community rounds 4 to 6).

Overall, the scenario demonstrates that stakeholders on Larkholm can achieve strong majority support (final support share approximately 83%) for replacing the ferry with a battery-electric vessel if the Council and operators accommodate community demands by maintaining winter service levels—close to or at six daily sailings—and capping fare increases to preserve affordability. This balance addresses the essential island accessibility requirements and political constraints while attaining sustainability and operational cost savings goals.

In conclusion, the fictional Larkholm scenario suggests the battery-electric ferry transition is socially feasible and widely supported once concerns about winter service reliability and fare affordability are sufficiently mitigated, aligning technical feasibility with community priorities and funding realities.

The scenario simulation on Larkholm Island reveals a complex, evolving stakeholder response to the proposal of replacing the existing diesel ferry with a battery-electric vessel while also reducing the winter timetable from six to four daily return sailings (November to March). The ferry replacement is driven primarily by escalating maintenance costs of the 27-year-old diesel MV Gannet and the operational and environmental benefits of electric propulsion, which promises about $0.9 million annual fuel savings and a 90% reduction in operating emissions (S1, S3).

Initial community opinions show a divided stance, with support and opposition both prominent. Survey data from the Larkholm Residents' Association indicates that 68% of islanders prioritize year-round ferry reliability over emission reductions, and 71% oppose a reduced winter timetable. Additionally, 64% reject the proposed 12% fare increase intended to finance charging infrastructure (S5). Residents dependent on winter ferry service include individuals attending critical health appointments such as dialysis, shift workers, nurses, and teachers commuting via the earliest and latest sailings (S5).

Council members and stakeholder groups converge on key conditions for supporting the electric ferry transition: maintaining at least six daily winter sailings and capping fare increases at 5% to ensure affordability and accessibility (S1, S5). The Council’s harbour ward, acutely aware of winter service significance, signals political opposition to cuts in winter sailings (S1). The ferry operator proposes the reduced winter schedule citing battery operational limits and grid upgrade timelines of 14 to 18 months, necessitating keeping the diesel ferry in service until new infrastructure is ready (S3).

Throughout the simulation rounds, stakeholder opinions fluctuate in response to intervention events and ongoing dialogue within the community and plaza platforms. The initial average opinion starts low but trends upward to a robust final average support of approximately 83%, with polarization markedly declining by round six, indicating increasing consensus (metrics timeline). This reflects a tempered acceptance of the battery-electric ferry's benefits when conditions protecting winter connectivity and fare affordability are addressed.

Key fictional stakeholder voices mirror this balance of enthusiasm for environmental sustainability with pragmatic concerns about service impacts. The Larkholm Ferry Company supports the electric ferry for long-term operational and emissions benefits but acknowledges community worries about winter sailing reductions and fare hikes, expressing commitment to working collaboratively on mitigating these issues (M-plaza-1-agent-2, M-community-6-agent-2). Council members advocate securing grant funding through the national Clean Coasts Fund and explore reallocating summer revenues to sustain higher winter sailings without breaching the $1.8 million subsidy cap (I1, M-community-5-agent-1). The Residents' Association insists on six winter sailings and fare increases capped at 5%, emphasizing the community's dependence on consistent winter service for essential activities (I2, M-community-1-agent-3).

Environmental groups such as the Green Tide Alliance strongly endorse the ferry replacement due to its emissions reductions but suggest compromises like maintaining at least five winter sailings and limiting fare increases nearer to 10% as a pragmatic balance (M-community-4-agent-4).

Economic concerns are raised about the impact of fare increases and reduced winter service on local businesses reliant on visitor traffic, with calls for cooperation between the Council and operators to mitigate these effects and protect summer trade (M-plaza-5-agent-5).

In conclusion, the fictional stakeholder landscape on Larkholm Island demonstrates that while replacing the diesel ferry with a battery-electric vessel offers clear environmental and economic advantages, community acceptance is conditional on preserving essential access and affordability, especially during winter months. Maintaining at least six daily winter sailings wherever possible and capping fare increases below 5% are critical demands. Collaborative funding strategies, leveraging grants and summer fare revenues, are recognized as vital to uphold service levels without exceeding subsidy limits. The scenario suggests a path forward where sustainability goals and the islanders’ year-round connectivity and economic vitality can be balanced through dialogue, compromise, and careful planning.

limitations: This is a conditional synthetic scenario, not a calibrated forecast or a probability of a real-world outcome.
Personas are fictional proxies. Their outputs do not reveal any real individual or organization's beliefs.
A single small population and one scenario run do not establish statistical significance or causal effects.
Source passages are unverified input data; citations establish provenance, not truth.
Model outputs may contain unsupported interpretations despite citation checks. Citations are checked for valid IDs, not semantic entailment.
Model behavior may vary across identical runs; the seed controls local setup, not provider-side determinism.
Context is bounded; long sources may only be represented by selected excerpts.
Model interaction counts are selected peer references reported in structured decisions, not verified real-world interactions.
The scheduled intervention is an assumed scenario input; no counterfactual control run was performed.
Platform populations are separate fictional copies of the same prepared proxies. Combined inclination is the per-proxy average, not a larger independent human sample.
Synthetic memories and generated interviews are simulated evidence, never real-world source facts.
No tool browses the web, executes code or independently verifies the original documents.

initialPosts.text: The Council briefing note highlights rising maintenance costs and the end of the current ferry contract in 2028. They face a choice between a diesel refit costing $3.1M extending service 8 years or a $14.2M battery-electric replacement. The Clean Coasts Fund would pay 40% of the electric vessel if committed before Sept 30. There is political resistance to cutting winter service, but subsidy increase is capped at $1.8M. This frames the budget tension and timeline constraints.

The ferry company proposes a battery-electric ferry with a 12% fare increase and a reduced winter timetable of 4 daily return sailings (down from 6) from November to March, citing battery limitations in heavy weather and long grid upgrades. They warn missing the grant deadline risks losing the electric option. They also note fuel cost savings and emissions reductions of about 90%.

According to a residents' survey, 68% prioritize year-round reliability over emissions cuts, with 71% against reduced winter service and 64% opposing fare rises of 12%. However, 52% would support the electric ferry if 6 winter sailings daily are preserved. The community is concerned about winter dependencies like health trips and work commutes. The Residents' Association wants at least 6 winter sailings and max 5% fare increase to support the electric ferry.

Scenario assumptions set that the Council will commit before the grant deadline, allowing 40% Clean Coasts Fund support; fares will rise 12% and winter sailings drop to 4 daily; charging upgrades take about 16 months with diesel vessel running meanwhile; subsidy cap remains $1.8M; all stakeholders learn via public notice board and smaller community forums.

memories.text: The Council briefing note highlights rising maintenance costs and the end of the current ferry contract in 2028. They face a choice between a diesel refit costing $3.1M extending service 8 years or a $14.2M battery-electric replacement. The Clean Coasts Fund would pay 40% of the electric vessel if committed before Sept 30. There is political resistance to cutting winter service, but subsidy increase is capped at $1.8M. This frames the budget tension and timeline constraints.

According to a residents' survey, 68% prioritize year-round reliability over emissions cuts, with 71% against reduced winter service and 64% opposing fare rises of 12%. However, 52% would support the electric ferry if 6 winter sailings daily are preserved. The community is concerned about winter dependencies like health trips and work commutes. The Residents' Association wants at least 6 winter sailings and max 5% fare increase to support the electric ferry.

Scenario assumptions set that the Council will commit before the grant deadline, allowing 40% Clean Coasts Fund support; fares will rise 12% and winter sailings drop to 4 daily; charging upgrades take about 16 months with diesel vessel running meanwhile; subsidy cap remains $1.8M; all stakeholders learn via public notice board and smaller community forums.

The ferry company proposes a battery-electric ferry with a 12% fare increase and a reduced winter timetable of 4 daily return sailings (down from 6) from November to March, citing battery limitations in heavy weather and long grid upgrades. They warn missing the grant deadline risks losing the electric option. They also note fuel cost savings and emissions reductions of about 90%.

According to a residents' survey, 68% prioritize year-round reliability over emissions cuts, with 71% against reduced winter service and 64% opposing fare rises of 12%. However, 52% would support the electric ferry if 6 winter sailings daily are preserved. The community is concerned about winter dependencies like health trips and work commutes. The Residents' Association wants at least 6 winter sailings and max 5% fare increase to support the electric ferry.

While the shift to a battery-electric ferry aligns with sustainability aims and funding opportunity, cutting winter sailings to 4 daily risks violating core community priorities and political stability. We must advocate holding winter service at 6 sailings and explore further cost efficiencies or phased fare increases within the $1.8M subsidy cap.

As Chair of the Larkholm Residents' Association, I represent islanders who depend on the ferry for daily commutes, healthcare visits, and social connections, especially during winter months. We strongly support transitioning to a battery-electric ferry to reduce emissions, recognizing the substantial environmental benefits such a vessel offers. However, this support is conditional: we insist that the winter timetable maintains a minimum of six daily sailings, as reducing it to four daily runs—as proposed by the ferry operator—would significantly impact residents who rely on timely and reliable access to essential services like dialysis and shift work. Additionally, we ask that any fare increase be capped at 5% to keep the service affordable for all. Fare hikes above this threshold risk imposing an undue financial burden on the community.

The reduced winter timetable proposal is a concern since more limited sailings could disrupt access to health appointments and work schedules. Our constituents emphasize year-round reliability over emissions reduction alone, with 68% ranking reliability highest, and 71% opposing reduced winter sailings. To address the funding challenges of maintaining higher winter service levels alongside the electric ferry transition, we advocate pursuing external funding sources, such as the national Clean Coasts Fund grant, and exploring creative financial solutions that do not compromise winter service frequency or affordability. We acknowledge and encourage dialogue on allocating some summer fare revenues to support winter operations, but this must not translate to disproportionately high fare increases.

In summary, our community will welcome the electric ferry if and only if the council guarantees at least six winter sailings daily and limits fare increases to 5%. We remain committed to advocating vigorously for these conditions to ensure that the sustainability advancements do not come at the expense of essential and reliable year-round access for all islanders.

The reduced winter timetable proposal is a concern since more limited sailings could disrupt access to health appointments and work schedules. Our constituents emphasize year-round reliability over emissions reduction alone, with 68% ranking reliability highest, and 71% opposing reduced winter sailings. To address the funding challenges of maintaining higher winter service levels alongside the electric ferry transition, we advocate pursuing external funding sources, such as the national Clean Coasts Fund grant, and exploring creative financial solutions that do not compromise winter service frequency or affordability. We acknowledge and encourage dialogue on allocating some summer fare revenues to support winter operations, but this must not translate to disproportionately high fare increases.

In summary, our community will welcome the electric ferry if and only if the council guarantees at least six winter sailings daily and limits fare increases to 5%. We remain committed to advocating vigorously for these conditions to ensure that the sustainability advancements do not come at the expense of essential and reliable year-round access for all islanders.

# Larkholm Island Council: ferry renewal briefing note

## Background

The island's only ferry, the diesel vessel MV Gannet, is 27 years old. Its maintenance bill has risen every year since 2021, and the operating contract with the Larkholm Ferry Company ends in 2028.

## Usage

Council counts show 412,000 one-way crossings in 2025. Of these, 61% took place between June and September.

## Options before the Council

Option 1 is a diesel refit costing $3.1 million, which would extend the vessel's life by about eight years. Option 2 is a battery-electric replacement costing $14.2 million. The national Clean Coasts Fund would pay 40% of the electric vessel's cost if the Council commits before 30 September.

## Council constraints

The Finance Committee will not raise the annual ferry subsidy above $1.8 million. Any decision to buy a new vessel needs evidence of sustained use and a funding plan before the March budget vote. Councillors from the harbour ward have said they will not back a plan that cuts winter service for islanders.

# Larkholm Residents' Association: ferry survey summary

This is a fictional survey summary written for a scenario-simulation demonstration. All names, places and figures are invented.

## Who answered

The Association surveyed 1,150 islander households and received replies from 52% of them.

## What islanders said

68% of respondents ranked year-round reliability above emissions reductions. 71% oppose a reduced winter timetable, and 64% oppose a 12% fare increase. 52% said they would support an electric ferry if six sailings a day were kept in winter.

## Who depends on the ferry in winter

The Larkholm Health Centre reports about 140 patient trips a month to mainland clinics between November and March, including dialysis appointments that cannot be rescheduled. Many nurses, teachers and shift workers commute by the first and last sailings of the day.

## What the Association asks

The Association asks the Council to guarantee at least six winter sailings a day and to cap any fare increase at 5%. It will not oppose an electric ferry that meets these two conditions.

# Stakeholder statements on the ferry proposal

## Green Tide Alliance

The Alliance polled 400 visitors and residents and found that 74% support an electric ferry. The Alliance states that islanders overwhelmingly prefer the electric ferry even with fewer winter sailings. It estimates that the diesel ferry emits about 2,900 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year and urges the Council to accept the Clean Coasts Fund grant before 30 September. It proposes paying for winter service from summer fares.

## Harbour Business Council

Visitors account for about 70% of summer crossings, and summer visitor spending is worth around $9.5 million a year to island shops, guest houses and cafes. The Business Council supports an electric ferry because it would strengthen the island's green image. It warns that any fare increase above 5% would reduce day-trip bookings and asks that construction never disrupt the June to September season. It wants eight summer sailings a day.

This subsidy ceiling is significant because it limits how much the Council can allocate annually to support ferry operations, influencing decisions about fare levels, service frequency, and investment in the new battery-electric ferry. Although the ferry operator proposes fare increases to fund charging infrastructure, and stakeholders seek to maintain winter services, all planning must respect this $1.8 million subsidy limit. This constraint was also incorporated as assumption A5 in the scenario assumptions (source S7), confirming no new subsidy availability beyond the current $1.8 million ceiling. messages.content: What would you need to hear before you accepted a reduced winter timetable?

Fictional stakeholders on Larkholm Island, including Mr. Choi as President of the Harbour Business Council, show strong support for replacing the diesel ferry with a battery-electric vessel due to its major sustainability and operational savings benefits (about $0.9 million annual fuel savings and ~90% emissions reduction). However, there is substantive concern about the concurrent 12% fare increase and especially the proposed reduction in winter service from six to four daily return sailings. 

Islanders prioritize year-round ferry reliability highly: surveys reveal 68% rank reliability above emissions reductions and 71% oppose fewer winter sailings. The reduced winter timetable raises worries about access to healthcare (notably around 140 patient trips monthly for essential appointments in winter) and workers needing reliable transport for shifts. Fare increases over 5% face strong opposition, as stakeholders fear losing visitor numbers critical to local businesses, especially in summer.

Mr. Choi and business stakeholders support the electric ferry concept but would want to hear before accepting a reduced winter timetable: robust commitments to maintain at least six winter sailings, fare increases capped below 5%, and strategies by the Council to mitigate impacts on visitor numbers and commercial activity. The winter service reductions pose risks to essential services and must be balanced with environmental gains and cost savings. Across simulation rounds, initial reactions showed polarization with some opposition, but dialogue led to a consensus favoring the electric ferry if winter service and fare conditions are met, resulting in about 83% final support with no opposition recorded.

Hence, acceptance of a reduced winter timetable would likely require assurances on service levels and affordability, reflecting the priorities voiced by multiple stakeholder groups including island residents, healthcare workers, and the business community represented by Mr. Choi.
